title: Finding what's nearby: cells, trees and distances
dek: "Restaurants that deliver to me" and "the nearest free rider" are questions an ordinary index can't answer well, because nearness is in two dimensions. Here is how geohashes, quadtrees, hexagon grids and R-trees turn them into fast lookups, and how static places differ from riders who move every few seconds.

items: Computing the distance to every restaurant works for thousands, not for lakhs of searches a second over crores of places. Divide the map into cells and look only in the few cells near the customer.
Geohashes name square cells by a string; nearby places share a prefix, but places on either side of a border don't, so always search the cell and its 8 neighbours.

Quadtrees adapt cell size to density; hexagon grids give every neighbour the same distance; R-trees (PostGIS) handle shapes such as delivery zones. Moving riders belong in memory, not in a disk index.
Nearness needs latitude and longitude together. A B-tree on (lat, lng) narrows by latitude well, then has to scan every longitude in that band.
Checking every place is fine for a few thousand restaurants; at 10,000 searches a second over lakhs of restaurants it is crores of distance calculations a second.
The fix in every method below is the same: map positions to cells or boxes, fetch the few near the customer, then measure real distances on that small set.

body.cap: Every extra character divides the cell into 32. The length you index decides how many cells a search touches.

items: A geohash interleaves the bits of longitude and latitude and writes them in base 32, so `tek92e` is a cell about 1.2 by 0.6 km in central Pune.
Places in the same cell share the prefix, so an ordinary string index finds a cell's places: `WHERE geohash6 = 'tek92e'`.

The catch is the border: a restaurant 50 m away in the next cell has a different prefix. Search the cell and its eight neighbours, then sort by true distance (the Restaurants near me problem draws this).
Cells near the poles get thin and the grid isn't uniform, which matters little for a delivery app in one country.

body.label: ZOTATO · A GEOHASH SEARCH IN SQL
body.x:
-- restaurants carry geohash6, indexed; the customer is in tek92e
SELECT id, name, lat, lng FROM restaurants
WHERE geohash6 IN ('tek92k','tek92s','tek92u',
                   'tek927','tek92e','tek92g',
                   'tek926','tek92d','tek92f')   -- the cell and its 8 neighbours
  AND open_now;
-- then compute the real distance for these few rows and keep those within 3 km
body.say: A query for restaurants whose six-character geohash is the customer's cell, tek92e, or one of its eight neighbours, and that are open now. The application then computes the real distance for these few rows and keeps those within 3 kilometres.

body.cap: A fixed grid wastes cells on empty land and overloads cells in the busy centre. A quadtree splits only where the restaurants are.

body.x: Restaurants rarely deliver in a perfect circle. Store each delivery zone as a polygon and ask which zones contain the customer: `ST_Contains(zone, point)` with a GiST index, or precompute which cells each zone covers and look up the customer's cell.

items: Restaurants never move; riders move every few seconds. With 2 lakh riders online, a disk index would be updated tens of thousands of times a second: the wrong tool.
Keep each rider's latest position in memory, in a map from cell to riders (or Redis geo commands), and update the cell when the rider crosses a border.
Expire riders who stop sending pings, so a phone that died doesn't stay 'nearest' for ever.
Straight-line distance only shortlists. Rank the shortlist by travel time from a routing service, because a river or a one-way street can make 500 m a 15-minute ride.

items: Say the two-step shape: cells to find candidates, then real distance or travel time to rank them.
Pick a cell size from the search radius, and mention the border fix (neighbouring cells).
Separate static places (an index in the database) from moving ones (latest positions in memory).
Use polygons when delivery areas aren't circles.
Where it appears here: the Restaurants near me problem builds the static side; Rider dispatch keeps moving riders in a grid in memory.

body.label: Go deeper: k nearest, not just within a radius

body.x: 'Within 3 km' is easy with cells. 'The 5 nearest riders' is harder, because you don't know how far to look. Start with the customer's cell and its neighbours; if fewer than 5 riders turn up, widen to the next ring of cells, and stop once the fifth-nearest found is closer than any unsearched cell could be. R-trees and PostGIS answer k-nearest directly with `ORDER BY location <-> point LIMIT 5`.
